entry.evidence: The size of the microglacier is well monitored, but information about its thickness is sparse.

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML full text (jats_text) of tc-16-4847-2022

steps.action: Cite earlier borehole depths of Snezhnika: Popov (1957) reached ground at 8 m, and Gruenewald et al. (2006 boreholes) estimated 11 m.
steps.quote: bored into the middle part of Snezhnika and reached ground at 8 m

steps.action: Take from the literature the idea that perennial snow patches and microglaciers indicate and preserve local mountain permafrost.
steps.quote: Perennial snow patches contribute to local permafrost occurrence and aggradation because they work as a shield with relatively high albedo

steps.action: Take from published field studies the expectation that frozen ground shows a marked rise in resistivity and that ice reduces GPR reflections.
steps.quote: A marked increase in resistivity at the freezing point has been shown in several field studies

steps.action: State the aim: the thickness and internal structure of Snezhnika, the subsurface of its bed, and where its meltwater goes.
steps.quote: The aim was to investigate the thickness and internal structure of the Snezhnika microglacier and the subsurface structure near it

steps.action: Design the survey: GPR lines across and along the slope; 24-electrode Schlumberger ERT lines 30-40 m long at 1.5 m spacing that stay inside the moraine; parameters taken from European permafrost surveys.
steps.quote: The lengths of the profiles were chosen to have the maximum length and depth of study while not having to cross over the moraine ridge

steps.action: Acquire nine GPR radargrams in 2018 and 2020 with a 270 MHz antenna and apply a standard processing chain (dewow, bandpass, gain, background removal).
steps.quote: 270 MHz antenna model 5104A by GSSI, Inc., USA

steps.action: Acquire ERT data on one, two and three profiles in 2018, 2019 and 2020 on the ice-free lower bed; add a UAV terrain model and GPS positions.
steps.quote: ERT measurements near Snezhnika were conducted in 2018, 2019, and 2020 along one, two, and three profiles, respectively.

steps.action: Time the field campaigns for the end of summer, before first snow, when the glacieret is expected to be smallest; weather prevented the same date each year.
steps.quote: The time of measurements was chosen to be at the end of the summer and before the first snow in the mountain

steps.action: Convert the 2018 radargrams to depth with standard-table velocities and estimate ice thickness (1-2 m in the lowest part to 5-6 m upslope) and the depth of the drained bed layer.
steps.quote: The uppermost layer represents the microglacier.

steps.action: Interpret the reflection-poor pocket-like recesses in the third GPR layer as ice lenses or ice-rich ground.
steps.quote: it is assumed that the pocket-like structures are ice lenses or ice-rich areas

steps.action: Estimate ice thickness on the two 2020 along-slope GPR profiles: 4-7 m on GPR(2020)-1 and about 8 m on GPR(2020)-2.
steps.quote: the relief of the lower surface is clearly traced at a depth of about 8 m

steps.action: Check the 2020 depths against the 2018 depths where GPR(2020)-1 intersects GPR(2018)-4 and -5; both give about 7 m.
steps.quote: The obtained depths of Snezhnika in 2020 correlate very well with the results obtained in 2018.

steps.action: Compare the maximum thickness with borehole depths: it agrees with Popov's 8 m but does not reach Gruenewald's 11 m or Onaca's 12 m.
steps.quote: The obtained maximum thickness of the microglacier shows agreement with the results from early borehole measurements

steps.action: Attribute the mismatch to incomplete GPR coverage and to boreholes giving only point information, rather than revising the thickness estimate.
steps.quote: this can be a reason for not observing a depth greater than 8 m

steps.action: Invert the ERT-1 data for 2018-2020 with RES2DINV and identify three resistivity zones, the deepest above 60 000 Ω m.
steps.quote: The deepest zone (Zone 3) is of greatest interest and is characterized by resistivity over 60 000 Ω m.

steps.action: Compare the Zone 3 resistivities with values published for ice and permafrost, and identify the zone as ice-rich permafrost.
steps.quote: [...] typical of ice and permafrost, and Zone 3 represents an ice-rich permafrost area.

steps.action: Propose from the low-resistivity Zone 2 that meltwater drains around the frozen zone, collects in the lowest part of the bed and sinks through karst.
steps.quote: then it flows deeper through a karst structure

steps.action: Repeat the test on ERT-2 in 2019 and 2020; a zone above 60 000 Ω m appears again in the southern part.
steps.quote: This zone appears with values of electrical resistivity over 60 000 Ω m and represents an ice-rich permafrost area in the base of the microglacier.

steps.action: Explain why the frozen zone lies about 1 m deeper in 2020 than in 2019 by interannual weather (Copernicus reports) and by slightly displaced profiles.
steps.quote: The sinking of the permafrost area in 2020 compared to 2019 is probably a result of two factors.

steps.action: Find Zone 3 again on the new ERT-3 line in 2020, then align the ERT-2 tomograms with the GPR(2018)-1 and -2 radargrams and show that the high-resistivity zone overlaps the reflection-poor zone.
steps.quote: In the aligned plot the high-resistivity zone fits well with the area identified as ice-rich permafrost on the GPR profiles.

steps.action: Keep the frozen zone, observed in each of three consecutive years, as evidence of permafrost under the definition of at least 2 years below 0 °C.
steps.quote: this can be treated as evidence of permafrost existence in high mountains (particularly the Pirin Mountains) in Bulgaria

steps.action: Propose two explanations: the ice is buried ice left by a larger Snezhnika, and it is preserved by shading from the Dzhamdzhiev ridge and the Vihren wall.
steps.quote: It might be buried ice, a remnant from Snezhnika when it had a bigger size for several consecutive years

steps.action: Support the shading explanation with the observed distribution: the zone and the thicker ice and snow are in the shaded south, and snow patches occur only at the foot of the ridge.
steps.quote: Proof of this assumption is the presence of snow patches, located at the bottom of the Dzhamdzhiev ridge, close to Snezhnika.

steps.action: Explain the deeper top of the frozen zone in 2020 than in 2018 by the smaller glacieret, less shading, interannual weather and shifted profiles.
steps.quote: This change in depth is probably due to several factors such as the lack of shading from the glacieret

steps.action: Place the finding in the regional picture: permafrost probably occurs above about 2400 m in Pirin (after Oliva et al. 2018 for Rila), sporadic in the cirque.
steps.quote: Permafrost probably exists above ∼ 2350 m in the Rila Mountains and above ∼ 2400 m in the Pirin Mountains.

steps.action: Keep the thickness estimate: mean about 4-6 m, up to 8 m in the south, with the caveat that coverage is incomplete.
steps.quote: The mean thickness estimated from GPR profiles is about 4–6 m.

steps.action: Keep the headline claim: an ice-rich permafrost zone in the southern bed, detected by GPR and ERT and in every ERT campaign.
steps.quote: This can be taken as evidence of permafrost in the Pirin Mountains.

sequences.source_document: Open discussion record of tc-2021-337 (RC1, AC1, RC2, AC2)

steps.action: Referees asked about measurement dates and weather timing; the authors added exact dates and the end-of-summer timing rationale (§2.3 ¶5).
steps.quote: It would also be helpful to mention the precise date of geophysical measurements each year.

steps.action: Referee 1 objected to radargrams without topography; the authors reprocessed the radargrams with topography and equalized the layer velocities.
steps.quote: The topography is added to the radargrams according to comments from Referee1.

steps.action: The question was narrowed to the Snezhnika microglacier: the Banski Suhodol site was removed, 'perennial snow patches' became 'microglacier', and the title was changed.
steps.quote: since is not the subject of this paper you should avoid referring to this site when presenting the aim of the paper

steps.action: The abstract was revised to say the thickness may exceed 8 m ('reaching 8 m or probably more').
steps.quote: Maximum thickness of ice can be higher than 8 m in the upper part of the glaciaret where there are no transversal profiles.

steps.action: The claim's wording was changed from 'frozen zone' to permafrost or ice-rich permafrost.
steps.quote: replace `frozen zone` with permafrost/ice-cemmented sediments.

steps.action: A comparison with the 12 m depth of Onaca et al. (2022) was added to the discussion and conclusions.
steps.quote: according to Onaca et al., 2022 the maximum dept was 12 m. You should also refer to this finding.

steps.action: In the rebuttal only, the authors computed how a velocity of 0.16 instead of 0.15 m/ns changes thickness (about +0.54 m at the deepest point).
steps.quote: The change from 0.15 m/ns to 0.16 m/ns (+0.01 m/ns) will add 6.7 cm to every meter from the glacier section.

steps.action: Request for differential GPS answered without new data: handheld GPS accuracy defended, geodetic GPS deferred to future work.
steps.quote: When doing geophysics in such a rough terrain the protocol says that differential GPS is mandatory!

steps.action: The point that non-repeated GPR lines prevent quantifying change was acknowledged; no repeated profiles exist.
steps.quote: It means that you can not actually compare the radargrams, by means of changes.

steps.action: Request for upper-glacieret GPR profiles in 2018 answered by citing the steep slope; no new data.
steps.quote: [...] would have been good to try at least 1 or 2 GPR profiles in the upper part of the glaciaret in 2018

steps.action: Request for 5 m electrode spacing and a profile across the moraine declined; 1.5 m spacing defended for resolution and the moraine judged unsafe.
steps.quote: Using a smaller distance between the electrodes we have better resolution.

steps.action: Concern about ERT electrodes in snow answered by clarification only: just one electrode on one profile was in debris-covered ice.
steps.quote: This was possible due to the shape of the microglacier and boarder between the ice and the gravel.

steps.action: The 'ice lenses' were reinterpreted as ice-rich permafrost or a mixture of ice and rock, with layer velocities equalized in Table 2.
steps.quote: I think here might be rather an ice-rich permafrost

steps.action: Asked to explain the year-to-year deepening of the frozen zone, the authors added an auxiliary explanation in the paper (Copernicus weather, profile displacement).
steps.quote: Can you explain why the active layer has thickened so much in only 1 year?

steps.action: A paragraph on GPR and ERT limitations, non-uniqueness and rugged-terrain errors was added (§1 ¶10).
steps.quote: Please write a paragraph on the methodological uncertainties (mainly the limitations of GPR and ERT)

steps.action: Factors other than shading were acknowledged as possible controls on permafrost preservation (§3.2 ¶7, §4 ¶4).
steps.quote: Indeed, shading is essential, but is not acting alone.

tree.answer: A high-resistivity, reflection-poor zone under the southern bed of the microglacier
No; inferred from GPR depth conversion and ERT inversion
Estimate ice thickness and the structure of the bed
Rivals only loosely named (frozen rock blocks or older ice; buried ice); no systematic set
No distinct predictions derived for the rivals
Conditions found in end-of-summer field campaigns

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Three annual campaigns repeat the observation
Zone recurs across years and profiles and co-locates on GPR and ERT
Kept as evidence of ice-rich permafrost; thickness 4-6 m mean, up to 8 m
Accepted after major revisions; wording, interpretation and limitations revised, design requests declined

end.claim: A zone above 60 000 Ω m with no GPR reflections in the southern bed of Snezhnika, detected in every campaign from 2018 to 2020, is interpreted as ice-rich permafrost, the authors' first indication of permafrost in the Pirin Mountains.

decisive_move.sentence: Detecting the high-resistivity zone in each of three consecutive years, and matching it on GPR and ERT, is what lets the authors invoke the at-least-2-years definition of permafrost.

gates.evidence: The survey aim was thickness and structure (§1 ¶11), although the ERT parameters were chosen 'for optimal results when observing permafrost' (§2.3 ¶1). The frozen zone could have failed to recur across campaigns or to match between GPR and ERT, but no temperature measurement tests the permafrost (temperature) definition directly. Nothing was fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: UAV structure-from-motion terrain model (7.63 cm/px) used for profile positions and elevations
Handheld Garmin GPS for profile coordinates and glacier outlines
Dielectric polarization and displacement currents in ice as the basis for the resistivity and radar contrasts

novelty_claims.quote: These results imply for the first time the existence of permafrost in the Pirin Mountains and in Bulgaria.
The results from the first detailed geophysical investigations of the Snezhnika glacieret
No publications have been found that investigate the long-term state of the frozen subsurface in high mountains in Bulgaria.
One of the main results from the study is a more comprehensive large-scale assessment of the ice thickness than has [...] .

limits: Permafrost is defined by temperature, but no ground temperature or borehole data are presented; the claim rests on resistivity values and reflection patterns compared with literature values. Referee 2 noted that Onaca et al. (2020, 2022) had already indicated permafrost in Pirin, so the 'first time' claim is contested in the review record. GPR lines were not repeated between years and ERT lines were only approximately repeated, so changes are not quantified. Positions come from handheld GPS improved with UAV images. GPR velocities are taken from standard tables; the effect of the velocity choice is computed only in the rebuttal (AC2-S p.5), not in the paper. That rebuttal check is listed in v_checks as performed_here (inference: it was done by the authors but is not published). Sub-claims and their statuses: ice thickness, estimate_with_resolution (4-6 m mean, 8 m maximum, no formal uncertainty given); meltwater drainage through karst, best_explanation (weak, only proposed); shading as the preservation control, best_explanation, with other factors acknowledged; buried-ice origin, speculative. Coding trace_series is approximate (inference): rivals are hardly stated, and the walk is close to applying a capability to an unstudied site. Whether meteorological records informed the interpretation beyond the Copernicus reports is not shown. The abstract's 'in the 2 years' and the conclusion's '3 consecutive years' are inconsistent in the text.

disagreements.target: Gruenewald et al. (2008) borehole depth of 11 m
disagreements.support: The GPR profiles detect at most 8 m; the authors attribute the gap to incomplete coverage and to boreholes being point measurements.
disagreements.quote: [...] depth of 11 m obtained by is not detected.

disagreements.target: Onaca et al. (2022) depth of 12 m to the ice-gravel boundary
disagreements.support: The authors accept 12 m as probably the maximum thickness but note their profiles do not cross that area.
disagreements.quote: but the depths of 11 m and 12 m are not detected

alternatives_considered.chosen: Standard-table GPR velocities (ice 0.15, gravel with ice 0.13, limestone 0.12 m/ns)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Velocities from borehole reference values or a velocity model built from the radargrams

alternatives_considered.chosen: ERT profiles 30-40 m long at 1.5 m spacing, kept inside the moraine
alternatives_considered.reason: The moraine ridge was unstable and dangerous to climb; field width and safe electrode access

alternatives_considered.chosen: New GPR lines in 2020 placed to cover more of the glacier
alternatives_considered.reason: To cover more area and estimate thickness in more places; most 2018 lines were off the glacier in 2020
Harsh weather prevented acquisition on the same date

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Frozen, well-joined rock blocks or older ice for the 4-8 m layer on GPR(2020)-2
